input.quote: 7.2 Before engaging another provider, Customer must disclose and match for Vendor any more favourable commercial offer it receives.
input.rationale: Section 7.2 (the first of two provisions numbered 7.2) binds Customer, not Vendor: we cannot engage another provider unless we first disclose any more favourable offer and match it for Vendor. That is a de facto right of first refusal that restrains our freedom to source elsewhere for the entire term, with no product-category limitation, no 12-month sunset, and no automatic termination on Vendor's service-level or delivery failure — so it fails the fallback and sits close to walk-away exclusive dealing. It also directly contradicts Section 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no exclusivity or most-favoured-customer commitment. Redline deletes the restraint and states Vendor's non-exclusive status, consistent with the preferred position; the fallback (defined category, 12 months, performance-based exit) is offered in the comment. Flagged here because the clause independently breaches this rule as a sourcing restraint, distinct from any pricing analysis.

ops.oldText: 7.2 Before engaging another provider, Customer must disclose and match for Vendor any more favourable commercial offer it receives.
ops.newText: 7.2 Vendor is a non-exclusive provider of the Services. Customer may engage any other provider at any time, without notice to Vendor and without any obligation to disclose or match any other offer.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We removed the requirement to disclose and match third-party offers before engaging another provider, as it operates as an open-ended exclusivity/right of first refusal on our sourcing and contradicts Section 12.3, under which we make no exclusivity commitment. Our playbook position is that Vendor is non-exclusive; if some restraint is needed we could consider one limited to a defined service category for 12 months, ending automatically on any service-level or delivery failure.
proposal.summary: Replace the match-before-sourcing obligation with express non-exclusivity.
